item.title: ‘Hard Art’ Asks Hard Questions About Daring to Be Abstract
item.description: MoMA PS1 brings together more than 40 Black artists in a search for their historical and artistic ties.
item.dc:creator: Aruna D’Souza
item.media:credit: Julius Frazer for The New York Times
item.media:description: Artists in “Hard Art” include (left to right) standing: Suzanne Jackson, Rindon Johnson, Eric N Mack, Tiona Nekkia McClodden, Torkwase Dyson. Seated: James Little, Howardena Pindell, Charisse Pearlina Weston.

item.title: The Geezer of Graffiti Art, Barry McGee, Goes ‘Another Round’ in Los Angeles
item.description: From train yards to Jeffrey Deitch, a luminary of street art cuts “another hole in the fence” bringing his friends to his new exhibition.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Griffin
item.media:credit: Jack Bool for The New York Times
item.media:description: Barry McGee in front of an untitled sculpture made from fanned surfboards for his new show at Jeffrey Deitch. The graffiti artist still aims for his work to be inclusive of underrepresented voices.

item.title: She Commands the Sunken Titanic, From 1,000 Miles Away
item.description: A Virginia judge, empowered by quirks in maritime law, has overseen the salvage of the remote shipwreck for decades. Now her rule is being challenged.
item.dc:creator: Marc Davis
item.media:credit: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group, via Getty Images
item.media:description: When it sailed from Europe in 1912, the Titanic’s majesty and reputation for opulence brought attention to its maiden voyage.

item.title: The Rocky Rise of Max Levai, Art World Nepo Baby
item.description: The gallerist fits the stereotype of the art world scion. But in reality he had to start (almost) from scratch.
item.dc:creator: Nancy Hass and Marisa Chafetz
item.media:description: Max Levai, gallerist and owner of The Ranch in Montauk, N.Y., on a 60-foot-tall sculpture, “Meditating Figure,” by Matt Johnson that led to a lawsuit with the town.

item.title: Nara, Recorder of Japanese Girlhood, Finds New Freedom in Color
item.description: In interviews in New York and Washington, on the eve of two major shows, he discloses the effect of glaucoma on his work.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Solomon
item.media:description: Yoshitomo Nara, “Green Song,” 2026. In the painting — acrylic on canvas, and over 7 feet tall — her hair is a mosaic of orange and ocher squares.

item.title: Kehinde Wiley Will Debut New Art Series
item.description: The artist, who has been facing sexual misconduct allegations, became a single father in May and returns to the gallery world this week with a new show, “What the Light Becomes.”
item.dc:creator: Zachary Small
item.media:description: The artist Kehinde Wiley in his Brooklyn studio in October.

item.title: ‘It Gave Me a Lot of Anxiety’: Alex Katz on Sharing the Room With Matisse
item.description: At 99, the American painter confronts his lifelong reverence for the modern French master in a rare double billing at the Matisse Museum.
item.dc:creator: Roslyn Sulcas
item.media:credit: Rebecca Marshall for The New York Times ; artworks: Succession Henri Matisse/ARS, Alex Katz/ARS
item.media:description: “Odalisque With a Red Casket” (1927) by Henri Matisse and “Reclining Bather” (1960) by Alex Katz at the Matisse Museum in Nice, France.

item.title: An Artist Who Won’t Avert Her Gaze From Violence
item.description: Teresa Margolles grapples with the traces of murder and disappearance. A survey at MoMA PS1 connects her projects in Mexico since the 2000s, and the United States today.
item.dc:creator: Siddhartha Mitter

item.title: Lucien Smith, Art-World Star, Died From Accidental Drug Overdose
item.description: Shortly before Mr. Smith died, he created a series of new “Rain Paintings” that are now on display in a show at the Tripoli Gallery in Wainscott, N.Y.
item.dc:creator: Derrick Bryson Taylor and Leila Sheridan
item.media:description: The artist Lucien Smith in New York City in 2016.

item.title: Whitney Museum Announces Curators for 2028 Biennial
item.description: Meg Onli, a Biennial veteran, and Zack Winokur, the former artistic director of Little Island, will organize the 83rd edition of the much-scrutinized exhibition.
item.dc:creator: Mariah Kreutter

item.title: A Rembrandt on Your Skin: Museum Hosts a Tattoo Parlor in Amsterdam
item.description: For two weeks, patrons at the Rembrandt House can get tattoos of the artist’s drawings and etchings, courtesy of “the godfather of Amsterdam tattoo culture.”
item.dc:creator: Nina Siegal
item.media:credit: Ilvy Njiokiktjien for The New York Times
item.media:description: The tattoo artist Henk Schiffmacher holding Rembrandt’s etching “The Descent from the Cross,” which he has been tattooing across Bo Kwakernaak’s back, in Amsterdam.

item.title: A Conceptual Artist Entwines Her Work With the State
item.description: How Jill Magid made the government her publisher and her artistic collaborator.
item.dc:creator: Julia Halperin and Amina Gingold
item.media:description: “I feel like my piece is a public artwork embedded in a public square,” Jill Magid said of having her artwork, “With Full Consent,” embedded in the Federal Register.

item.title: Why Does Culture Feel So Monotonous? A Walking Tour Reveals the Math.
item.description: The data scientist Lauren Leek says predictive algorithms are flattening the everyday world, from pub menus to pop lyrics.
item.dc:creator: Scott Reyburn
item.media:credit: Joanna Yee for The New York Times
item.media:description: Chain storefronts on a London street reflect what Lauren Leek calls the “flattening” of modern consumer culture.

item.title: Art Gallery Shows to See in November
item.description: This week in Newly Reviewed, Andrew Russeth covers Gedi Sibony’s scavenger hunt, Mildred Thompson’s vivid planets, Fiona Tan’s voices and ghosts, and Ben Kinmont’s archives.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Russeth
item.category: The Renee and Chaim Gross Foundation

item.title: A Museum’s ‘Wanted’ Poster Campaign Brings Looted Painting Back to France
item.description: The Orléans Fine Arts Museum is on a quest to recover hundreds of works stolen during World War II — and the director wants your help.
item.dc:creator: Ephrat Livni
item.media:description: Among the Italian masterpieces sought by the Orléans Fine Arts Museum in France is a Madonna and Child attributed to Lorenzo Costa.

item.title: Kit Kemp Shares 5 Things She Wishes She’d Made
item.description: The designer Kit Kemp on five big ideas she wishes she could claim as her own.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Dunn

item.title: Designers Find Inspiration in Folklore, Symbols and Rituals
item.description: Throughout the world, creators are finding inspiration in folklore and putting new twists on archaic symbols and rituals.
item.dc:creator: Ali Morris

item.title: How an Italian Capital of Design Is Coping with Climate Change
item.description: Some of Milan’s best creative minds are working on solutions to floods, drought and 100-degree days.
item.dc:creator: Laura Rysman
item.media:credit: Pontus Berghe for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Porta Nuova district of Milan with the Unipol Tower, at right, designed by the architect Mario Cucinella. It has an elliptical form, a mostly opaque double-skin facade and an atrium to buffer temperature fluctuations and reduce energy consumption.

item.title: A Photographer and His Young Son Create a Fresh Take on Still Lifes
item.description: The photographic collection called Nino + Dad represents a multigenerational collaboration that offers a fresh take on still lifes.
item.dc:creator: Julie Lasky

item.title: How a Villa Near Lake Como Became a Crowd Pleaser
item.description: The family treasure was sumptuous enough to host a pope in the 17th century, but for guests today, air-conditioning would enhance the appeal.
item.dc:creator: Laura May Todd and Andrea Wyner
item.media:description: A bedroom in the Villa Raimondi, portions of which date to 1452, where Pope Innocent XI is said to have slept in the late 17th century.

item.title: A Belgian-Congolese Designer Finds Her Muse in Music
item.description: “Hearing different kinds of rhythms and tones makes me understand shapes better,” said Kim Mupangilaï.
item.dc:creator: Ben Dreith and Katherine Marks
item.media:description: Kim Mupangilaï in her Brooklyn studio, near her Banda chaise. “I always need music to design,” she said. “Hearing different kinds of rhythms and tones makes me understand shapes better.”

item.title: A Parisian Townhouse Is Transformed into an Art Nouveau Museum
item.description: Hector Guimard’s Hôtel Mezzara is being prepared for its future life as a museum dedicated to Art Nouveau.
item.dc:creator: Eve M. Kahn and Joann Pai
item.media:description: Hôtel Mezzara, a townhouse in the 16th arrondissement in Paris that was commissioned in 1910 for the textiles tycoon Paul Mezzara and his family. It is being converted into the Musée Guimard, dedicated to Art Nouveau.

item.title: Many of Trump’s Plans to Remake D.C. Would Push Locals Aside

item.dc:creator: Michael Kimmelman and Alex Kent

item.dc:creator: Kurt Soller and Lucile Casanova

item.description: The photographer Allan Sekula explored the hidden world of global shipping from the perspective of dockworkers and sailors in this celebrated series debuting in New York.
